edition.deck: Nvidia faces congressional scrutiny after Jensen Huang’s abrupt exit; Ukraine’s peace talks widen as Europe seeks a place at the table.
edition.editorialNote: Prioritises overnight developments and consequential reporting across international affairs, UK public life and Danish domestic news. Returning subjects are included only where the fresh gather adds a material development or angle.

content.headline: Nvidia’s Jensen Huang quits as Congress summons him over spy claims
content.shortHeadline: Nvidia’s Huang quits as Congress summons him
content.standfirst: The company’s co-founder has stepped down as CEO and board member amid reports of multiple affairs, including one with a woman suspected by US officials of links to Chinese intelligence. The allegations remain unresolved.

image.caption: Jensen Huang has resigned as Nvidia’s chief executive.

sources.originalTitle: Ex-Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang summoned to testify before Congress about affair with alleged Chinese spy
Jensen Huang resigns as Nvidia CEO after alleged affairs
A timeline of the affair scandal that sank Nvidia’s Jensen Huang
Who is Colette Kress, interim Nvidia CEO after Jensen Huang exit?

segments.body: Jensen Huang has resigned immediately as Nvidia’s CEO, president and board member. The company named chief financial officer Colette Kress as interim CEO and is searching for a permanent successor. Huang has been summoned to testify voluntarily before a Senate committee on 3 December; House committees have also requested a closed-door interview.

segments.title: The allegations and the stakes
segments.body: The affair reports have prompted scrutiny of national-security risks because Alice Huang, a Singapore-based businesswoman and Nvidia customer, is suspected by US intelligence officials of being a Chinese asset. China has rejected that claim as a smear. The US attorney general says the Justice Department has reached no conclusion about whether she engaged in espionage.

segments.title: A leadership test for Nvidia
segments.body: Nvidia’s board had commissioned an independent investigation into the relationship. The company says it has no reason to believe national security or company secrets were compromised. Its shares have fallen sharply this week, while analysts differ over how difficult it will be to replace Huang’s technical leadership.

perspectives.body: The Guardian’s report on interim CEO Colette Kress highlights questions about whether a finance chief can sustain Nvidia’s technical risk-taking, alongside accounts of her deep operational experience and the board’s confidence in her.

content.headline: Ukraine welcomes European role in peace talks as prisoner swap is agreed
content.shortHeadline: Europe invited into Ukraine talks as prisoner swap is agreed
content.standfirst: US envoys say European delegates will join the next round of negotiations. Moscow has not softened its territorial demands, and the proposed exchange—described as the largest since Russia’s 2022 invasion—has no published timetable or confirmed number.

image.caption: US envoys Jared Kushner and Steve Witkoff met Volodymyr Zelensky in Dublin.

sources.originalTitle: Zelensky welcomes US bringing Europe into Russia-Ukraine peace talks
Ukraine war briefing: Europe to join negotiations, says Kushner, as Putin warns against peace keepers
Kushner ser ingen fredsaftale om Ukraine uden Europa ved bordet
OVERBLIK: Det ved vi om mødet mellem Putin og USA’s udsendinge i Moskva

segments.body: Volodymyr Zelensky welcomed a US pledge to include European delegates in the next round of talks with Russia, saying Europe needs a voice in negotiations that will shape its security. Jared Kushner and Steve Witkoff met Zelensky in Dublin after talks with Vladimir Putin in Moscow.

segments.title: A possible exchange, but no breakthrough
segments.body: Russia and Ukraine agreed to another prisoner exchange. Kushner said it could reunite thousands of people, but the number and timing have not been announced. Putin said Russia’s position on the war and its territorial demands had not changed; he also warned against European peacekeeping troops in Ukraine.

perspectives.body: DR reports that Danish Prime Minister Mette Frederiksen sees no sign that Russia wants peace. Its EU correspondent says other European leaders in Dublin voiced similar doubts about Moscow’s willingness to negotiate.

segments.title: Pressure on the battlefield
segments.body: Zelensky said restrictions were affecting Ukraine’s access to Starshield, SpaceX’s military satellite service, and its ability to intercept Russian drones. Russia and Ukraine also reported fresh drone attacks and casualties, while a Ukrainian agricultural company said it had suspended operations at its oilseed plants after Russian strikes.

content.headline: Ebola response in DR Congo falters as millions in aid go unaccounted for
content.shortHeadline: Ebola response falters amid questions over aid spending
content.standfirst: Médecins Sans Frontières says unpaid, under-equipped and poorly trained frontline teams are struggling to contain an outbreak that has killed more than 5,400 people. The charity is calling for stronger oversight of funds already disbursed.

image.caption: MSF says many frontline workers lack the equipment they need.

sources.originalTitle: Millions of Ebola dollars missing with staff unpaid while virus spreads, charity says

segments.body: Médecins Sans Frontières says essential supplies are scarce, some ambulances have run out of fuel and frontline workers are going unpaid as Ebola continues to spread in DR Congo. The outbreak, declared in May, has infected 11,000 people and killed more than 5,400, according to the report.

segments.title: Where the money went
segments.body: Africa CDC said last month that $700m of $962m disbursed to organisations responding to Ebola was unaccounted for, describing the issue as a major transparency and financial-reporting failure—not evidence of embezzlement. MSF is urging the Congolese government and UN agencies to improve oversight; the BBC says it has sought comment from the government.

segments.title: Barriers to containing the outbreak
segments.body: MSF says contact tracing is deeply problematic and reports that two-thirds of deaths are occurring in communities rather than treatment centres. Conflict, poor roads and shortages of basic supplies complicate the response. The Bundibugyo strain has no approved vaccine or treatment, although trials are under way.

content.headline: Ethiopian forces take Tigray towns, but residents report continued fighting
content.shortHeadline: Tigray fighting continues despite army control of key towns
content.standfirst: Federal forces rapidly took Mekelle and other main towns after fighting resumed in September. Residents and military sources say clashes continue elsewhere, while the TPLF calls its withdrawal a strategic retreat and says it is preparing to fight back.

image.caption: Pro-government forces marched into Tigray’s capital less than two weeks after the fighting began.

sources.originalTitle: Neither war nor peace in Tigray - is Ethiopia's latest conflict really over?

segments.body: Ethiopia’s national army has taken control of most of Tigray’s main towns, including the regional capital, Mekelle, after fighting resumed in late September. Hundreds of people are reported to have died. The BBC says it cannot report from the region and has been unable to independently verify accounts of events there.

segments.title: Competing accounts of what comes next
segments.body: Government supporters say the war is effectively over. The Tigray People’s Liberation Front says its withdrawal from towns was deliberate and claims it is preparing a counteroffensive. Residents describe continued fighting, including artillery and drone strikes; analysts disagree on whether the TPLF can sustain a wider conflict.

segments.title: Fear and uncertainty
segments.body: The return of troops has revived fears left by the 2020–22 war, which was marked by widespread abuses and allegations of ethnic cleansing. Residents told the BBC that their priority is peace and the chance to rebuild, while analysts say political and economic grievances remain unresolved.

content.headline: Trump says US no longer needs an Iran deal and redirects Vance
content.shortHeadline: Trump says US no longer seeks an Iran deal
content.standfirst: The president says negotiations are unnecessary and has told Vice-President JD Vance to focus on domestic issues. The shift appears to leave a standoff in place, with a US blockade of Iranian ports and no final agreement.

sources.originalTitle: Trump says no deal needed on Iran war and orders Vance to focus on domestic issues

segments.body: Donald Trump said the United States no longer needs a deal with Iran and directed JD Vance, who had been involved in efforts to restart talks, to focus on domestic issues. The move marks a shift in the administration’s approach to the war, which began with US and Israeli strikes on Iran in February.

segments.title: A stalemate without a settlement
segments.body: The US continues a blockade of Iranian ports, while the Strait of Hormuz has mostly reopened to shipping, including crude-oil shipments. Trump has described the war as effectively over and says a further military escalation is not necessary, though he has also said US forces are ready to act.

content.headline: Eight killed in Brooklyn building collapse as investigators examine construction
content.shortHeadline: Eight dead after Brooklyn building collapses beside worksite
content.standfirst: Six adults and two children died and 18 people were injured when a three-storey building fell into a neighbouring construction site. Officials say the cause is not yet known and are investigating whether any criminal conduct contributed.

sources.originalTitle: What we know about Brooklyn building collapse that killed eight people

segments.body: A three-storey building in Brooklyn’s Flatbush neighbourhood collapsed on Wednesday, killing eight people and injuring 18. Rescue operations ended the following day after officials concluded there were no more victims at the site. Four of the injured were firefighters; one person remained in critical condition.

segments.title: Investigation under way
segments.body: The building fell into a neighbouring construction pit. Officials say it is too early to determine the cause or whether construction played a part. The Department of Buildings said no code violations had been reported at the residential building before the collapse; police and the district attorney are investigating whether any criminal conduct contributed.

content.headline: Ukrainian drone hits Russian warship in Gulf of Finland, officials confirm
content.shortHeadline: Russian warship hit by Ukrainian drone in Gulf of Finland
content.standfirst: Finnish officials confirmed an attack on the Russian vessel Naro-Fominsk, apparently near the Ust-Luga port. The extent of damage and any casualties are unclear; Finland says the Baltic remains safe for civilian shipping.

image.caption: The Russian vessel Naro-Fominsk is believed to have returned towards St Petersburg after the attack.

sources.originalTitle: Russian warship hit by Ukrainian drone in Gulf of Finland

segments.body: Finnish officials confirmed that a Russian warship was attacked in the Gulf of Finland on Wednesday. Ukraine’s SBU says it targeted the Naro-Fominsk during a wider drone operation against Russia’s Ust-Luga oil-export depot. Estonia’s defence minister said the ship was seen smoking and headed back towards St Petersburg.

segments.title: What remains unknown
segments.body: The extent of damage to the ship and whether there were casualties have not been confirmed. Finland’s foreign minister said the Baltic Sea situation remains stable and that there is no threat to marine traffic. A military analyst quoted by the BBC called the strike unprecedented in this part of the Baltic but not a serious escalation.

content.headline: FBI says North Korean hackers stole $400m using fake video calls
content.shortHeadline: FBI links fake video-call scams to $400m crypto theft
content.standfirst: US authorities say a scheme called FaceStealer targeted more than 900 people in cryptocurrency and web3, using counterfeit video meetings to install malware. The FBI says the North Korean regime uses large-scale crypto theft to fund its weapons programme.

image.caption: The FBI released redacted examples of videos it says North Korean hackers used in the scheme.

sources.originalTitle: North Korean hackers used fake video calls in $400m crypto hack, says FBI

segments.body: The FBI says North Korean state-backed hackers stole more than $400m in cryptocurrency over 18 months using a scheme it calls FaceStealer. More than 900 victims are thought to have been targeted, particularly people working in cryptocurrency and web3.

segments.title: How the scam works
segments.body: US authorities say hackers use fake or hijacked social-media accounts to invite targets to video calls on counterfeit versions of services such as Zoom and Teams. A recording is played to make the call seem genuine; a false audio-fix prompt then tricks the target into downloading malware that can expose contacts and accounts.

content.headline: UK economy grows 0.7% as AI investment boosts services
content.shortHeadline: AI investment helps UK economy grow 0.7%
content.standfirst: The economy expanded at its fastest quarterly pace in two and a half years, led by services and IT. Analysts warn that higher inflation, energy bills and interest rates could test that momentum.

image.caption: The UK recorded 0.7% quarterly GDP growth in the third quarter.

sources.originalTitle: AI helps UK economy grow at fastest pace for more than two years
AI helped UK defy expectations – but will economy’s resilience fizzle out?

segments.body: UK GDP rose 0.7% in the third quarter, its strongest quarterly growth since early 2024, according to the Office for National Statistics. Services grew 0.9%, with information and communications up 2.1%; the ONS said businesses linked to AI and cloud computing reported some of the largest increases in turnover.

segments.title: Growth faces headwinds
segments.body: Construction contracted, with private housebuilding well below its 2022 high. Economists say AI-related investment and data-centre activity have supported growth, but warn that higher inflation and interest rates, alongside rising household energy bills, may weigh on businesses and consumers in the months ahead.

perspectives.body: The Guardian’s analysis cautions that the growth is vulnerable if the AI investment boom slows, while an expected rise in winter energy bills could put further pressure on household spending.

content.headline: Microsoft outage disrupts Outlook and Teams as recovery efforts falter
content.shortHeadline: Microsoft struggles to restore Outlook and Teams
content.standfirst: Thousands of users reported problems across Microsoft 365 services for more than nine hours. Microsoft says it has no indication of a cyberattack and is investigating server-configuration issues after initial fixes failed.

image.caption: The Microsoft outage affected services including Outlook and Teams.

sources.originalTitle: Microsoft struggles to fix huge outage affecting Outlook and Teams
Microsoft Outlook er nede i store dele af verden

segments.body: Microsoft 365, Outlook, Teams and other services were disrupted across multiple countries, with Down Detector recording nearly 130,000 reports at the peak. Microsoft said the problems may stem from server settings and that restored servers became unavailable again when traffic returned.

segments.title: A wider dependency
segments.body: Microsoft says Exchange services, which underpin Outlook, were among the most affected; Teams chats and meetings were less disrupted. Connectors used by OpenAI and Anthropic were also affected. Microsoft has ruled out a cyberattack based on the information it has so far and says recovery may be gradual.

content.headline: MI5 will need evidence to regain judges’ trust after Agent X case
content.shortHeadline: MI5 must prove its claims to judges after Agent X case
content.standfirst: Investigatory powers commissioner Lord Leveson says courts are likely to demand proof from the security service after an inquiry found serious failures and false evidence about an abusive informant.

image.caption: Lord Leveson said judges may require evidence before accepting future claims from MI5.

sources.originalTitle: MI5 will need proof to be believed in future, says Leveson after BBC investigation

segments.body: Lord Leveson, who oversees the conduct of MI5, said judges would be more reluctant to accept the service’s claims without supporting evidence after the Agent X case. A secret inquiry found that MI5 gave false evidence to three courts about its handling of the violent neo-Nazi informant.

segments.title: Changes and accountability
segments.body: The inquiry found serious and systemic failures, including that a senior officer repeatedly lied. MI5 has apologised and accepted the findings. New policies address agents and domestic abuse or coercive control, and MI5 has changed how it prepares evidence. The High Court declined to pursue contempt proceedings and said police may be better placed to take the case forward.

content.headline: UK and EU near reset deal, with medicine-supply cooperation proposed
content.shortHeadline: UK-EU reset deal nears agreement, including medicine talks
content.standfirst: Negotiators say agreements on food trade, emissions and youth mobility are close, while a proposed health-security arrangement would improve information-sharing on medicine shortages. Access to the EU’s Made in Europe scheme and student fees remain unresolved.

image.caption: Andy Burnham met European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen in Dublin.

sources.originalTitle: Burnham says 'win-win' deal can be agreed between UK and EU
UK on cusp of historic Brexit deal as hopes grow last obstacle can be overcome
Antibiotic and ADHD drug shortages set to be eased under new Brexit deal

segments.body: UK and EU negotiators are seeking agreements on food and drink trade, carbon markets and youth mobility ahead of a 20 November summit. A UK source described the package as 95% complete, but leaders have stressed that a deal is not done and some questions could remain after the summit.

segments.title: Conditions still in play
segments.body: The UK is seeking access to the EU’s proposed Made in Europe scheme. An EU diplomat told the i Paper that inclusion is likely if Britain follows through on an offer to lower tuition fees for EU students and agrees to raise tariffs on Chinese electric vehicles. The two sides also differ over how much say the UK would have on EU rules it adopts.

segments.title: A proposed health-security arrangement
segments.body: A draft statement also proposes a health-security agreement to share information about medicine shortages and where supplies may be sourced. A Nuffield Trust expert called this a significant first step, but the arrangement is still being negotiated and does not itself guarantee that shortages will be avoided.

perspectives.body: The i Paper’s health-policy reporting identifies medicines including antibiotics, ADHD and epilepsy treatments among areas affected by shortages, and notes that supply problems have multiple causes, including global disruption and post-Brexit barriers.

content.headline: Capture scandal: Court of Appeal to review another Post Office conviction
content.shortHeadline: Post Office Capture conviction referred to appeal court
content.standfirst: The Criminal Cases Review Commission says there is a real possibility that Narinder Aujla’s 1998 theft conviction could be overturned because of new evidence about faulty Post Office software.

image.caption: The government commissioned an independent review of the Post Office Capture system.

sources.originalTitle: Man jailed over Post Office Capture scandal could get conviction quashed

segments.body: The Criminal Cases Review Commission has referred Narinder Aujla’s conviction to the Court of Appeal, saying there is a real possibility it will be quashed. Aujla served four months in prison after being convicted of theft in 1998 over losses at his Dudley Post Office branch.

segments.title: A separate software scandal
segments.body: The case concerns Capture, an accounting system used before Horizon. An independent review found it could cause unexplained losses, and a compensation scheme has paid at least £8.5m to hundreds of people. Those with criminal convictions must first have them overturned to receive compensation.

segments.title: More cases under review
segments.body: The CCRC says it has received 40 applications linked to Post Office prosecutions predating Horizon. Twenty-one were rejected, 12 remain under review and three Capture-related convictions have now been referred to the appeal court. The Post Office says it will assist the independent court.

content.headline: UK appoints climate-security adviser as report warning remains unpublished
content.shortHeadline: UK names climate-security adviser as key report stays secret
content.standfirst: Madeleine Alessandri, a former head of the Joint Intelligence Committee, will advise the government on climate-related security risks. The Guardian says a report she helped lead, warning of threats including food shortages and migration, remains unpublished in full.

image.caption: Andy Burnham arrives at the Cop31 climate summit in Antalya.

sources.originalTitle: UK appoints world’s first special representative for climate security
UK ministers have no plans to publish explosive report on climate crisis

segments.body: Prime Minister Andy Burnham appointed former Joint Intelligence Committee chair Madeleine Alessandri as the UK’s special representative for climate security. She will advise on risks that climate change and nature loss may pose to national security, including pressure on food supplies, infrastructure and communities.

segments.title: The report still under wraps
segments.body: Alessandri led a report warning that ecosystem collapse overseas could bring food shortages, higher prices, migration and conflict. The Guardian reports that the government has no plans to publish the full report; a redacted version was released earlier. The government was contacted for comment.

segments.title: Questions over policy
segments.body: Burnham told the climate summit that the UK remains committed to net zero by 2050. Campaigners have questioned that commitment, citing support for new fossil-fuel projects and possible changes to electric-car requirements. The International Energy Agency’s head told the Guardian that Burnham supports electrification.

perspectives.body: The Guardian’s reporting contrasts Burnham’s summit pledges with critics’ concerns about domestic energy decisions, while also recording the International Energy Agency chief’s view that the prime minister supports electrification.

content.headline: Under-25 benefit changes could replace health payments with work support
content.shortHeadline: Proposed youth welfare changes could replace health payments
content.standfirst: Alan Milburn’s forthcoming review is expected to recommend a new pathway for young people without severe work-limiting disabilities instead of the £217-a-month Universal Credit health element. The proposals are not yet final government policy.

sources.originalTitle: Under-25s with ADHD or anxiety set to see £217 a month disability benefits axed
‘No one wants to see cuts’: Labour MPs sound alarm over youth benefits reforms

segments.body: A review led by Alan Milburn is expected to recommend that some under-25s receive education, training and employment support instead of the health element of Universal Credit, worth £217 a month to new claimants. The i Paper reports that Prime Minister Andy Burnham and Work and Pensions Secretary Pat McFadden are expected to consider the proposals.

segments.title: Support, conditions and concerns
segments.body: The review is expected to favour a more locally tailored system, with support linked to participation in work, education or training and priority help for some vulnerable young people. Labour MPs have warned that reducing benefits could leave disabled young people worse off; others say the proposals deserve a hearing. The review has not yet been published.

perspectives.body: The i Paper reports sharp concern among Labour MPs that benefit reductions, particularly for existing claimants, could penalise disabled young people; other MPs are open to the review’s employment-support proposals but say the details matter.

content.headline: US soldier arrested in UK was at NATO headquarters, report says
content.shortHeadline: US soldier arrested in UK had NATO-base role, report says
content.standfirst: A 41-year-old US service member is under investigation on suspicion of espionage-related offences involving Russia. Analysts say a NATO headquarters role could raise questions about access, but the material he may have accessed—and whether anything was passed to Russia—remains unclear.

image.caption: Imjin Barracks in Gloucestershire, where the soldier is reported to have been arrested.

sources.originalTitle: What we know as member of US Army arrested over ‘allegations of espionage’
The military secrets that could have been leaked by suspected US Army spy

segments.body: A 41-year-old US soldier was arrested in Gloucestershire under the National Security Act, in an investigation led by UK Counter Terrorism Policing with US authorities. The FBI says the allegations involve espionage related to Russia. Police have stressed that the investigation is ongoing.

segments.title: What access might mean
segments.body: The i Paper reports that the soldier was a lieutenant colonel based at Imjin Barracks, the UK headquarters of NATO’s Allied Rapid Reaction Corps. Analysts say such a role could involve insight into planning, readiness and allied decision-making, but caution that actual access depends on duties, clearance and need to know.

content.headline: Denmark’s tax deal cuts fuel duties but gives biggest gains to high earners
content.shortHeadline: Fuel-duty cuts in Denmark’s tax deal; biggest gains go to high earners
content.standfirst: The agreement with the Danish People’s Party would lower petrol and diesel duties for 2027 and phase out income-tax bands over several years. Analyses say the largest tax reductions are concentrated among higher earners; the package is not yet law.

image.caption: A Danske Bank analysis says the largest tax reductions go to higher earners.

sources.originalTitle: Bank har regnet på ny skatteaftale: De højest-lønnede vinder kæmpestort
Hvad betyder det for os, der tjener mellem 35-45.000 kroner om måneden og bor i lejlighed?': Eksperter svarede på jeres spørgsmål
Beregninger afslører vindere og tabere af ny skatteaftale
Det bliver dyrere – ikke billigere – at være pendler i 2027
Socialdemokratiet advarede mod billigere benzin - nu er det pludselig 'en rigtig god nyhed!'
Avisledere: Messerschmidt har solgt sig for billigt i skatteaftale

segments.body: The government and Danish People’s Party have agreed a package of tax changes, including a two-kroner-per-litre cut to petrol and diesel duties in 2027 and the gradual removal of the middle and top-top tax bands. The agreement is political, not yet enacted legislation.

segments.title: Who gains—and who may not
segments.body: PFA and Finance Ministry calculations indicate that higher earners stand to gain most from the income-tax changes, while people on more modest wages may see little direct benefit. The fuel-duty reduction is temporary. TV 2’s commuter analysis says some people with long journeys could lose more from the end of an enhanced travel deduction than they gain from cheaper fuel.

segments.title: A political trade-off
segments.body: The package also includes changes affecting student grants and unemployment benefits. Danish newspaper leaders criticised the Danish People’s Party’s deal, arguing that the temporary fuel-duty cut was a small return for its support. That is editorial criticism, not an assessment of the policy’s final effect.

perspectives.body: TV 2’s review of newspaper editorials finds several arguing that the Danish People’s Party accepted too little in return for its support, while one paper saw political value in the party showing it could make a deal independently.

content.headline: Women in Denmark still face long waits for menopause care, report finds
content.shortHeadline: Long waits persist for women seeking menopause care
content.standfirst: A TV 2 review found an average 15.8-week wait at the private gynaecology clinics listing waiting times, with some waits reaching a year. Clinicians say access and support vary by location, even as new guidance is being developed.

image.caption: A TV 2 graphic reports on access to care for menopause symptoms.

source.credit: Foto: Frederik Johan Scheel / TV 2 Grafik

sources.originalTitle: Nye retningslinjer gav håb, men kvinder mangler stadig hjælp

segments.body: TV 2’s review of listed waiting times found an average of nearly 16 weeks at 85 private gynaecology clinics, with some patients facing waits of up to 52 weeks. The report also describes women who say their symptoms were not recognised or addressed in primary care.

segments.title: Support and guidance
segments.body: A Rigshospitalet specialist says access differs across the country and that women should not have to wait months or seek costly private care to get help. New shared guidance for primary-care doctors is being prepared; professional groups differ on how readily the new hormone-treatment guidance can be applied in general practice.

content.headline: Man denies murder of former wife as court hears of repeated contact
content.shortHeadline: Man denies murder of former wife after repeated contact
content.standfirst: A 63-year-old defendant admits firing a gun but denies murdering his former wife in Brønshøj. The court heard evidence of repeated visits and hundreds of calls despite a restraining order; the trial is continuing.

sources.originalTitle: Tiltalt for skuddrab: Sov i bil foran ekskones bopæl trods tilhold

segments.body: A man accused of shooting his former wife to death in Brønshøj in 2025 has denied murder. He admits firing a gun but disputes how many shots he fired. The court heard that he had previously been subject to a restraining order and had repeatedly contacted or visited her.

segments.title: Evidence heard in court
segments.body: Prosecutors’ investigation found 807 calls over 68 days in the year before the killing, including 136 the day before and 30 on the day itself. The defendant told the court he had not intended to kill her. A mental assessment found he was not legally insane at the time, according to the report.

content.headline: Data breach exposes travel details of more than 144,000 Norwegian passengers
content.shortHeadline: Travel data breach affects more than 144,000 Norwegian passengers
content.standfirst: Norwegian says passenger information was exposed through a breach involving travel-technology provider Amadeus. A separate report says booking details of more than 350,000 SAS passengers may also have been affected.

image.caption: Norwegian and SAS passengers may be affected by a breach at travel-technology provider Amadeus.

sources.originalTitle: Over 140.000 Norwegian-passagerer berørt af datalæk

segments.body: A data breach exposed information on 144,249 passengers travelling with Norwegian and its subsidiary Widerøe, DR reports, citing a letter sent to Norway’s data-protection authority. The breach is believed to have begun in 2023 and involved access through Spanish technology provider Amadeus.

segments.title: Potential wider exposure
segments.body: NRK says the exposed information could enable unwanted contact, targeted phishing or other fraud. Norwegian says it is investigating whether the breach requires it to notify affected passengers. Separately, SVT has reported that booking information for more than 350,000 SAS passengers may have been exposed in the same breach.

content.headline: Dagrofa’s ABC Lavpris purchase approved, with wider Danish expansion planned
content.shortHeadline: Dagrofa wins approval to buy ABC Lavpris and expand
content.standfirst: The owner of Meny and Spar will take a majority stake in the Danish low-price chain from 1 December. Dagrofa says it aims to expand the brand beyond its current stronghold in Jutland and Funen.

image.caption: Dagrofa plans to expand the ABC Lavpris chain beyond its current regions.

source.credit: Foto: Bo Amstrup / Bo Amstrup / Ritzau Scanpix

sources.originalTitle: Meny-ejers køb af dansk kæde godkendt – skal bredes ud til hele landet

segments.body: The Competition and Consumer Authority has approved Dagrofa’s purchase of a majority stake in ABC Lavpris. The deal is due to take effect on 1 December. Dagrofa, which also owns Meny and Spar, says it wants to bring the chain to more parts of Denmark.

segments.title: Keeping a distinct offer
segments.body: ABC Lavpris has 16 stores, mostly in central and western Jutland, and sells about 5,000 products. A retail-sector expert says the format differs from discount chains by offering a wider range, and cautions that the chain may not match the very lowest prices. Dagrofa says it intends to preserve its identity.

content.headline: Greenland will return to its former time zone in October 2027
content.shortHeadline: Greenland to move clocks back an extra hour in 2027
content.standfirst: Greenland’s parliament has approved a return to UTC−3 from 31 October 2027, widening the time difference with Denmark by an hour. Some residents welcome the change; business and aviation effects remain a concern.

image.caption: Greenland’s parliament has approved a change to the territory’s time zone.

sources.originalTitle: Grønland rykker en time væk fra Danmark

segments.body: Most of Greenland has used UTC−2 in standard time since 2023. From 31 October 2027, the Inatsisartut decision will return the territory to UTC−3. When Denmark moves its clocks back, Greenland will move back by two hours, leaving it four hours behind Denmark in winter.

segments.title: Local time, wider connections
segments.body: A resident of Tasiilaq told DR he welcomed the move because the current time zone puts the sun out of step with midday. Greenlandic businesses have previously warned that a larger time difference could complicate business and air travel with Europe.

content.headline: Danish judges warn AI-generated legal filings could add to court delays
content.shortHeadline: Judges warn AI may be adding bulk to court filings
content.standfirst: A court president says some minor disputes now arrive as files of up to 120 pages. Judges cannot say AI is the cause, but warn that lengthy submissions and nonexistent case references can waste time and obscure key arguments.

image.caption: Inside the Eastern High Court in Copenhagen.

sources.originalTitle: Dommere advarer mod brug af kunstig intelligens

segments.body: The Danish Judges Association has warned that longer legal submissions may add to delays in an already pressured court system. A case that should take three or four pages can now run to 120, according to Jacob Waage, president of the Frederiksberg court.

segments.title: AI suspected, not established
segments.body: Waage said he cannot establish that artificial intelligence caused the increase. He has, however, seen filings containing unremoved AI prompts and references to court decisions that do not exist. Judges say longer documents make it harder to identify the relevant arguments and prepare cases.

content.headline: Repair cafés offer a growing local response to Denmark’s throwaway culture
content.shortHeadline: Repair cafés grow as Danes try to keep goods in use
content.standfirst: More than 150 Danish repair cafés now offer free help fixing household goods. A researcher says their effect on overall resource use remains small, but sees them as part of a wider shift towards repairable products.

image.caption: Volunteers at Repair Café Herlev help give electronics, clothing and other items a longer life.

sources.originalTitle: "Mirakelmager" gør op med dårlig vane, vi har haft i årtier

segments.body: Repair Café Herlev is among more than 150 repair cafés in Denmark, where volunteers help people fix items ranging from electronics and bicycles to clothing. In the past year, volunteers there examined 1,858 broken items and repaired them or found the fault in more than 82% of cases, according to the organisation’s records.

segments.title: A small part of a bigger change
segments.body: A researcher in circular economy says repair cafés still make only a small difference to total resource use, as the number of household devices continues to rise. He argues that wider change will also require political measures and products designed to last longer and be easier to repair.

content.headline: Kane breaks England caps record as victory over Croatia takes him to 126
content.shortHeadline: Kane reaches 126 caps as England beat Croatia
content.standfirst: Harry Kane scored the winner from the penalty spot on the night he became England’s most-capped men’s player. Morgan Rogers also defended Chelsea team-mate Cole Palmer amid questions about his commitment to the national side.

image.caption: Harry Kane became England’s most-capped men’s player.

sources.originalTitle: 'A lie' & 'nonsense' - Palmer committed to England, says Rogers
Kane scores winner but who else made an impression? England player ratings

segments.body: England beat Croatia 2-1 in the Nations League, with Morgan Rogers opening the scoring and Harry Kane converting a penalty for the winner. Kane’s appearance was his 126th for England, taking him past Peter Shilton’s previous men’s record.

segments.title: Rogers backs Palmer
segments.body: Rogers rejected suggestions that Cole Palmer is not committed to England, saying his Chelsea team-mate wants to represent his country but has also had to manage his body after injuries. Palmer was left out of the squad after manager Thomas Tuchel said he had missed too many chances to impress.

content.headline: Pochettino move gathers pace after Carrick’s Manchester United sacking
content.shortHeadline: United pursue Pochettino after Carrick sacking
content.standfirst: Manchester United have moved to activate a release clause in Mauricio Pochettino’s USA contract after dismissing Michael Carrick. Pochettino’s appointment is not yet complete, and the timing depends in part on the USA’s remaining fixtures.

image.caption: Mauricio Pochettino, appointed United States manager in September 2024.

sources.originalTitle: How Pochettino came on Man Utd's radar - and what Carrick was told when
The chaos that took Carrick from two-year deal to sacked within 15 games

segments.body: United dismissed Carrick on Thursday after a run of poor results and performances. The club have been in talks with Pochettino, and chief executive Omar Berrada contacted the US Soccer Federation to confirm the release clause and United’s intention to activate it. Pochettino has not yet been appointed.

segments.title: A difficult season and an uncertain timetable
segments.body: Carrick’s side conceded eight goals across defeats by Chelsea and Como and a draw with Aston Villa, while injuries and gaps in the squad also featured in BBC Sport’s account of his brief tenure. United want Pochettino in place quickly, but he is understood to be respecting the USA’s two matches against Haiti; if he takes charge of the second on 18 November, he is expected at United on 19 November.

content.headline: Crystal Palace sack Pierre Sage as talks with Thomas Frank advance
content.shortHeadline: Palace sack Sage as Frank talks advance
content.standfirst: Palace have dismissed their manager after five months, with the club bottom of the Premier League and struggling defensively. Thomas Frank is in advanced talks to take over, but no appointment has been confirmed.

image.caption: Pierre Sage’s time as Crystal Palace manager lasted five months and 16 games.

sources.originalTitle: Crystal Palace sack boss Sage after 16 games
Crystal Palace

segments.body: Crystal Palace have sacked Pierre Sage after five months and 16 games in charge. The club have lost four successive league matches, won two of their first 10 and conceded 24 goals. Three members of Sage’s coaching staff have also left.

segments.title: Frank the leading option
segments.body: Former Brentford and Tottenham manager Thomas Frank is in advanced talks and is viewed by Palace as the leading candidate, though the club has not confirmed a replacement. The club are bottom, but BBC Sport’s figures note that 37 of 88 teams with seven or fewer points after 10 Premier League games have gone on to stay up.

content.headline: Cummins calls Khawaja’s sandpaper claims ‘100% wrong’ and ‘utter nonsense’
content.shortHeadline: Cummins rejects Khawaja’s sandpaper claims
content.standfirst: Australia’s captain has forcefully denied Usman Khawaja’s claim that the whole team knew about the 2018 ball-tampering scheme. The dispute has reopened questions about the investigation and the accounts of those involved.

image.caption: Pat Cummins was named Australia Test captain in 2021.

sources.originalTitle: 'Wrong' and 'nonsense' - Cummins on Khawaja claims

segments.body: Pat Cummins said he did not know that sandpaper was being taken onto the field during Australia’s 2018 Test against South Africa, rejecting Khawaja’s claim that the entire team knew. Cummins called that assertion “100% wrong” and said there was no team meeting or wider plan to tamper with the ball.

segments.title: The dispute remains unresolved
segments.body: Khawaja has said the team should have taken responsibility, while David Warner has backed his account and criticised the original investigation. Cummins said Cricket Australia chief executive Todd Greenberg had reviewed the files and found the accounts consistent; Greenberg has said he sees no compelling reason to reopen the investigation.

content.headline: Grealish apologises to Everton fans after disciplinary absence
content.shortHeadline: Grealish apologises after Everton absence
content.standfirst: The on-loan midfielder has apologised after missing three Everton matches following a breach of club discipline. He returned in a behind-closed-doors win over Derby but has not yet played in front of Everton supporters since his absence.

image.caption: Jack Grealish is yet to record a goal contribution for Everton this season.

sources.originalTitle: Grealish apologises for absence after breach of discipline

segments.body: Jack Grealish apologised to Everton and the club’s fans for missing the side’s matches against Newcastle in the Premier League and Carabao Cup, and a win over Coventry, after a breach of club discipline. He returned on Thursday in a behind-closed-doors victory over Derby County.
Grealish said he loves playing for Everton and cannot wait to be back in front of the supporters. Manager David Moyes had previously said the club needed to wait and see how the issue developed.

content.headline: Arsenal hold Barcelona to a gritty draw at Camp Nou
content.shortHeadline: Arsenal earn gritty draw at Barcelona
content.standfirst: Arsenal ended Barcelona’s 100% Champions League record with a resilient 1-1 draw in Spain. The point gives Renee Slegers’ side seven from four matches and a boost after a difficult domestic season.

image.caption: Arsenal held Barcelona to a draw in the Women’s Champions League.

sources.originalTitle: Gritty Arsenal show different side in Barcelona draw

segments.body: Frida Maanum put Arsenal ahead against the run of play, and Caroline Graham Hansen equalised for Barcelona after the break. The hosts had almost 70% possession and 24 shots, but Arsenal held on for a draw that ended the European champions’ perfect start in the competition.

segments.title: A result to build on
segments.body: Arsenal have seven points from their first four matches and improved their chances of reaching the knockout stages. Manager Renee Slegers called the performance a “big boost” and praised the team’s grit, discipline and resilience as they seek to build on it.

content.headline: McIlroy starts strongly in bid for record-equalling Race to Dubai title
content.shortHeadline: McIlroy opens with three-under 69 in Dubai
content.standfirst: Rory McIlroy is two shots off the lead after a three-under opening round at the DP World Tour Championship. A win would give him an eighth Race to Dubai title and a fifth in succession.

image.caption: Rory McIlroy is chasing a fifth successive Race to Dubai title.

sources.originalTitle: McIlroy makes strong start in bid to equal Montgomerie's record

segments.body: McIlroy carded a three-under-par 69, with five birdies and two bogeys in windy conditions, to sit joint third after the first round. Joost Luiten leads on five under, one shot ahead of Jacob Skov Olesen and two clear of McIlroy.

segments.title: The season-long race
segments.body: McIlroy is seeking a fifth successive Race to Dubai crown and a record-equalling eighth overall. Leader Eugenio Chacarra opened with a level-par 72; only Chacarra and McIlroy can guarantee the season-long title by winning this week.

content.headline: Robertson set to equal Dalglish’s Scotland caps record against North Macedonia
content.shortHeadline: Robertson poised to match Dalglish’s 102 caps
content.standfirst: Andy Robertson is poised to win his 102nd Scotland cap at Hampden, drawing level with Kenny Dalglish’s record. If he plays in Monday’s match in Switzerland, he could move clear, but the milestone remains conditional.

image.caption: Andy Robertson is one of Scotland’s two men’s centurions.

sources.originalTitle: Robertson set to make history, but hero Dalglish will always be King
Scotland Men's Football Team

segments.body: Scotland captain Andy Robertson is set to match Kenny Dalglish’s record of 102 men’s caps if he plays against North Macedonia at Hampden on Friday. Robertson says Dalglish remains the greatest player Scotland has produced and that the occasion is about the team’s need to win.

Robertson could break the record in Monday’s Nations League match in Switzerland if he plays. He is one booking away from suspension, however, so a caution against North Macedonia could rule him out of that game.

content.headline: Cristale’s debut mixtape brings every side of the Brixton rapper into view
content.shortHeadline: Cristale puts her full story into her debut mixtape
content.standfirst: After weighing paths from football to university, the Brixton-raised rapper has finished her first full-length project. Clear Intentions ranges across grime, hip-hop and R&B, without guest artists to tell her story for her.

image.caption: UK rapper Cristale.

sources.originalTitle: ‘Young, Black and female in Brixton is hard’: ​from football to Top Boy and wordplay, the inspiring journey of UK rapper Cristale

segments.body: Cristale’s Clear Intentions is the 25-year-old rapper’s first completed full-length project, after two earlier attempts. The Brixton-raised artist says she made the mixtape a personal “mental audit”, drawing on relationships with herself, family, friends and work. She chose not to include guest artists: “I don’t feel like I need help telling this part of my story.”

segments.title: A path of her own
segments.body: Football, drawing and an architectural-design degree were among the possibilities Cristale considered before she committed to music. She says she faced assumptions about what a young Black woman from Brixton could achieve, while her parents encouraged her early recordings. Her sound has since expanded from drill to include grime, melodic guitar, hip-hop and R&B.

content.headline: Jane Wiedlin’s candid memoir revisits the Go-Go’s, fame and a difficult life
content.shortHeadline: Jane Wiedlin tells the story behind the Go-Go’s hits
content.standfirst: The Go-Go’s songwriter reflects on the pressures of fame, sexism in the music business and living with bipolar disorder. Her new memoir also describes painful experiences she says shaped her life and relationships.

image.caption: Jane Wiedlin.

sources.originalTitle: ‘My partners would all tell you I was a nut job’: Jane Wiedlin on the Go-Go’s, fame and the freedom of sex dungeons

segments.body: In TMI, Jane Wiedlin writes about the Go-Go’s and the life behind their bright power-pop hits. The band became the first all-female group to play its own instruments and write its own material to reach No 1 on the US album chart; Wiedlin says she wanted to tell her story without making herself look good or avoiding difficult subjects.

segments.title: Fame and its costs
segments.body: Wiedlin recalls that the band was often dismissed or sexualised by the music press, and says sexism shaped the way the Go-Go’s were treated. She also speaks about depression and bipolar disorder, and says she was diagnosed with bipolar disorder at 58. Her account includes an allegation that she was sexually assaulted as a minor by Rodney Bingenheimer; the Guardian says attempts to reach him for comment received no response.

content.headline: U2’s Carnaval de Luz finds the band sounding renewed and ready to reconnect
content.shortHeadline: U2 return to loud guitars on a newly confident album
content.standfirst: Their first album of new songs in almost nine years brings Larry Mullen Jr back to the drums and reaches for a more joyful, expansive sound. The band discuss how their shared decision-making shaped the record.

sources.originalTitle: U2: Carnaval de Luz review – rousing, restorative rock from a band ready to take on the world again
‘It’s a new world. It’s a little fascistic. And it needs a different response’: U2 on 50 years together – and why Bono can’t work with Trump

segments.body: U2’s Carnaval de Luz is their first album of new songs in almost nine years. The review hears a band revitalised by Larry Mullen Jr’s return to the drum kit, with loud guitars, spiritual themes and a renewed sense of purpose. It praises standout songs including “Street of Dreams” and “If the World Is at War We Better Not Be”, while noting that some lyrics retain Bono’s familiar earnestness.

segments.title: A band built on compromise
segments.body: In a separate interview, U2 describe their shared songwriting credits and committee-style decisions as a form of band democracy. They also discuss why Bono does not feel equipped to negotiate with the Trump administration, and say they still believe rock music can bring people together.

content.headline: Jorge Drexler’s journey from doctor to Oscar-winning songwriter
content.shortHeadline: Jorge Drexler finds freedom in music, movement and candombe
content.standfirst: The Uruguayan musician says it took decades to shake off the effects of growing up under a dictatorship that discouraged artistic expression. His new album returns to the candombe sound of home.

sources.originalTitle: ‘I didn’t dance until I was 45’: how Jorge Drexler went from repressed doctor to rump-shaking Oscar-winner

segments.body: Jorge Drexler trained as a doctor and began writing songs while working in medicine, before building a career as a singer-songwriter in Madrid. His song for The Motorcycle Diaries won the Academy Award for best original song in 2005, though he was not invited to perform at the ceremony. He sang it there anyway, delivering an a cappella version in place of an acceptance speech.

segments.title: Finding his rhythm
segments.body: Drexler says he grew up in Montevideo during a dictatorship hostile to musicians and artists, and “didn’t dance” until he was 45. His album Taracá returns to the candombe music of Uruguay and was nominated for eight Latin Grammys ahead of the awards on 12 November. He says the success of Spanish-language artists is widening the music’s reach.

content.headline: Sufjan Stevens gathers a sprawling history of Christmas songs into one set
content.shortHeadline: Sufjan Stevens’ Christmas songs find warmth in a new collection
content.standfirst: This compilation draws mostly on the singer-songwriter’s earlier holiday releases, with one new song. The review finds some odd choices but hears a consoling, communal spirit in the collection.

sources.originalTitle: Worst Christmas Ever!

segments.body: Worst Christmas Ever! collects songs from Sufjan Stevens’ earlier Christmas releases, adding one new track, “This Christmas (It Only Gets Better)”. The review questions some selections, including novelty treatments of “Holly Jolly Christmas” and “It Came Upon a Midnight Clear”, but finds the compilation’s strongest moments in the more intimate songs and their layered voices.

segments.title: A hand held out
segments.body: The new song’s lyrics admit to misanthropy before reaching towards hope: Stevens asks whether things will get worse, then suggests the Earth might improve. The review places the release in the context of his gradual return to public activity after the death of his partner, Evans Richardson, and his diagnosis of Guillain-Barré syndrome in 2023.

content.headline: Daine’s debut album turns a tangled industry story into fizzing pop
content.shortHeadline: Daine’s debut leaps between synth-pop, emo and alt-rock
content.standfirst: The Australian musician’s first album shifts between bright hooks and noisy, unsettled textures. The review finds flashes of emotional clarity amid a sound that keeps trying on new forms.

sources.originalTitle: In Endless Awe & Agony

segments.body: On In Endless Awe & Agony, Filipino Australian artist daine moves between synth-pop, alt-rock and hyperpop, with distorted recordings, chopped vocals and bursts of screaming. The review hears a clear step forward from daine’s earlier emo-pop work, particularly in the energetic “Love Love (Love Love)” and “PQC”.

segments.title: Searching for a shape
segments.body: The album reflects on exploitation, public image and the cost of success, themes that follow daine’s journey through the music industry and their departure from Warner Australia. The review finds that these ideas do not always form a coherent story, and that the album’s shifting influences can obscure its own identity. “(I Want You In) Dakota” stands out for its more direct scenes of longing and uncertainty.

content.headline: Skepta turns a long-awaited album into a reflection on legacy and belonging
content.shortHeadline: Skepta’s new album traces grime’s history and his own
content.standfirst: After years of delay, The Fork and Knife brings together grime, rap and dance music in a reflection on the artist’s career and family history. The review hears a portrait of immigrant Britain as well as an account of personal growth.

sources.originalTitle: The Fork and Knife

segments.body: Skepta’s first album in seven years begins with some familiar grime and rap gestures, but gradually widens its scope. The review hears him revisit earlier parts of his career while moving between collaborations with Aya Nakamura, Central Cee, Jorja Smith and Asake, before a nine-minute cypher that puts younger MCs alongside his own established style.

segments.title: A family story in the frame
segments.body: The album’s title recalls Skepta’s grandfather, a hospitality worker who wanted a better life for his children and grandchildren. The review reads that family history alongside the artist’s public identity as a grime musician, DJ and designer, arguing that the record tells a broader story of immigrant Britain.

content.headline: Amy Winehouse’s Back to Black remains powerful on its 20th-anniversary set
content.shortHeadline: Back to Black still hits hard in its anniversary edition
content.standfirst: A new multi-disc release adds a small number of previously unheard recordings to Amy Winehouse’s landmark breakup album. The review argues that the extras illuminate its making without filling the absence left by the singer’s death.

image.caption: Amy Winehouse, whose album Back to Black is marking its 20th anniversary.

sources.originalTitle: Back to Black (20th Anniversary Edition)

segments.body: The 20th-anniversary edition of Back to Black includes demos, B-sides and a live set alongside the original album. The review praises the record’s mix of 1960s-inspired arrangements and contemporary songwriting, and describes it as a defining breakup album whose personal detail and musical confidence still resonate.

segments.title: What the archive can and cannot add
segments.body: The new material traces the album’s development, including earlier versions of “Me & Mr Jones” and “Tears Dry on Their Own”. But the review notes that the set contains only five previously unheard tracks, and that the planned follow-up album’s demos were destroyed. The extras offer context, not a way to complete Winehouse’s short catalogue.

content.headline: NAZA documentary reaches more than 1.5 million viewers worldwide
content.shortHeadline: NAZA reaches 1.5 million viewers in cinemas worldwide
content.standfirst: The documentary about Israel’s surveillance of Palestinian civilians and killings in Gaza has played in 47 territories. A free global streaming release is planned for early December.

image.caption: A scene from the documentary NAZA.

sources.originalTitle: NAZA documentary on Gaza killings becomes one of year’s most watched

segments.body: NAZA, directed by Yuval Abraham and Rachel Szor and produced by the Guardian, had reached 1,547,033 viewers by 6 November, according to the film’s distributor data reported by the Guardian. It has played in cinemas across 47 territories and is among the most-watched documentaries with a theatrical release in 2026.

segments.title: A broad international run
segments.body: The film has drawn particularly large audiences in Italy, where it recorded 717,517 admissions, and has also played in the UK and Ireland, the Benelux, North America, France and Germany. The Guardian says a free, multilingual global streaming release on its website is planned for early December.

content.headline: Elsinore revisits Ian Charleson’s Hamlet performed while he was dying of Aids
content.shortHeadline: Elsinore tells the story of Ian Charleson’s final Hamlet
content.standfirst: A new film starring Andrew Scott recounts the actor’s 1989 National Theatre performance. People who knew Charleson describe the physical demands of the role and correct some of the drama’s departures from their memories.

sources.originalTitle: 'A hell of a thing to take on': The moving inside story of how Ian Charleson played Hamlet on stage while dying of Aids

segments.body: In 1989 Ian Charleson took over as Hamlet at the National Theatre after Daniel Day-Lewis left the production. Charleson was living with Aids, and completed 24 performances before his final show on 13 November. The forthcoming film Elsinore, starring Andrew Scott as Charleson, retells the story of that last major stage role.

segments.title: Memory and dramatic licence
segments.body: The BBC’s interviews with Charleson’s friend Sean Mathias, fellow actor Paul Jesson and doctor Margaret Johnson describe how his illness affected the performance and how the company supported him. Johnson says she did not advise him against taking the role, unlike the doctor character portrayed in the film; Jesson recalls that Charleson was physically weaker than Scott’s portrayal suggests.

content.headline: Ron Howard’s Avedon documentary explores the photographer’s restless eye
content.shortHeadline: Avedon documentary finds the people behind the portraits
content.standfirst: The Netflix film follows Richard Avedon’s six-decade career, from fashion photography to politically engaged portraiture. Its collaborators describe how conversation and trust helped him draw out his subjects.

image.caption: A still from the documentary Avedon.

sources.originalTitle: ‘I’m looking for faces which surprise me’: how Richard Avedon photographed the soul of his subjects

segments.body: Ron Howard’s documentary Avedon follows the photographer’s work across fashion, portraiture and political projects. The film uses material from the Richard Avedon Foundation’s extensive archives, including photographs, contact sheets and recordings of conversations in his studio.

segments.title: Portraits as collaboration
segments.body: Avedon’s former assistant Sebastian Kim and producer Dallas Brennan Rexer describe a photographer who treated sitters as creative participants, using conversation and playfulness to help them relax. The review highlights his portraits of Marilyn Monroe and his work with James Baldwin on Nothing Personal, alongside the political support he quietly provided to civil-rights activists.

content.headline: Give Me the Ball! recalls Billie Jean King’s fight for equality in tennis
content.shortHeadline: Billie Jean King’s fight for equality revisited
content.standfirst: This documentary follows King’s career as a champion and advocate for equal prize money, as well as the personal challenges that became public. The review praises its lively portrait but notes a missing voice from men’s tennis.

image.caption: Billie Jean King in Give Me the Ball!

sources.originalTitle: Give Me the Ball! review – tennis trailblazer Billie Jean King is ferocious force for equality

segments.body: Give Me the Ball! revisits Billie Jean King’s rise in women’s tennis and her campaign for equal rights and prize money. It also covers the high-profile 1973 “battle of the sexes” match with Bobby Riggs and the public revelation of King’s sexuality after her former partner sued her in the 1980s.

The review describes the documentary as engaging, with King herself among its interviewees and archival footage tracing her sporting and political significance. It also notes that no male tennis player appears to discuss her influence, an absence the critic finds surprising.

content.headline: 1 in 2 turns one film-maker’s bowel cancer treatment into a plea for earlier“
content.shortHeadline: 1 in 2 urges younger people not to dismiss cancer symptoms
content.standfirst: Film-maker David Wilkinson documents his own stage four bowel cancer treatment while asking why diagnoses are increasing among younger people. The film offers no clear explanation but stresses the cost of delayed diagnosis.

image.caption: Film-maker David Wilkinson in 1 in 2.

sources.originalTitle: 1 in 2 review – compassionate film about dealing with bowel cancer is a personal plea on behalf of the young

segments.body: In 1 in 2, film-maker David Wilkinson turns the camera on his own treatment for stage four bowel cancer and speaks with younger patients and NHS professionals. He asks why a disease once associated more with older people is appearing in younger age groups; the film raises diet, lifestyle and microplastics as possibilities but says there are no clear answers.

segments.title: The risk of being dismissed
segments.body: The review highlights accounts from younger patients who say their symptoms were initially misdiagnosed or written off. Wilkinson urges people not to delay using the bowel cancer test available by post, and the critic praises the film’s compassionate approach while retaining the uncertainty around why diagnoses among younger people are rising.

content.headline: Whispers in the Woods finds quiet wonder in a French forest
content.shortHeadline: Whispers in the Woods watches wildlife through a family’s eyes
content.standfirst: Vincent Munier takes his father and teenage son into the Vosges forest, where lynx, foxes and deer emerge from the shadows. The review praises a tender, visually stylised alternative to conventional nature documentaries.

image.caption: A scene from Whispers in the Woods.

sources.originalTitle: Whispers in the Woods review – paddling in the moonlight in tender study of human-animal interaction

segments.body: In Whispers in the Woods, director Vincent Munier brings his father Michel and teenage son Simon into the Vosges forest in eastern France. The film follows Simon as his grandfather introduces him to the local ecosystem, with lynx, foxes, deer and birds appearing in the winter landscape.

Rather than explain wildlife through a stream of facts or slow-motion footage, Munier often lets animals remain indistinct shapes behind branches. Warren Ellis’s score and the forest soundscape help create what the review calls a tender sense of awe, centred on the passing of knowledge between generations.

content.headline: Female Perversions gives Tilda Swinton an unconventional early US lead
content.shortHeadline: Tilda Swinton’s early US film still feels unusual
content.standfirst: Susan Streitfeld’s experimental 1996 film casts Swinton as a lawyer whose ambitions and erotic life unsettle conventional ideas of femininity. The review finds her performance singular and the film’s mix of sex and black comedy daring.

image.caption: Tilda Swinton in Female Perversions.

sources.originalTitle: Female Perversions review – Tilda Swinton searches for erotic adventures in rework of Madame Bovary

segments.body: In Susan Streitfeld’s Female Perversions, Tilda Swinton plays Eve, a successful lawyer whose relationship with a man, attraction to women and troubled memories complicate her public composure. The film draws on Louise J Kaplan’s study of sexuality and gender, but shifts its focus to a fictional character navigating desire and ambition.

The review describes the film’s theatrical scenes of sexual yearning and black comedy as an unusually experimental US debut for Swinton. It sees her performance as a sign of a screen presence resistant to conventional Hollywood roles.

content.headline: Tinto Brass, Italian director whose erotic films became cult favourites, dies at
content.shortHeadline: Tinto Brass, director of Caligula, dies aged 93
content.standfirst: The Italian director became best known for Caligula, a controversial film whose original release was reshaped by producer Bob Guccione. A later reconstruction brought more of the work closer to Gore Vidal’s screenplay.

image.caption: Director Tinto Brass.

sources.originalTitle: Tinto Brass obituary

segments.body: Tinto Brass, the Italian director known for erotic films including Salon Kitty and Caligula, has died aged 93. He began his career making work influenced by European art cinema, then became known for films that mixed eroticism, theatrical style and provocation.

segments.title: The film that followed him
segments.body: Caligula, starring Malcolm McDowell, Helen Mirren, Peter O’Toole and John Gielgud, was altered with additional scenes by co-producer Bob Guccione. Brass and screenwriter Gore Vidal asked to have their names removed from the credits. A 2023 version assembled from archival footage removed Guccione’s material and sought to move closer to Vidal’s original script.

content.headline: Walliams documentary lays out women’s allegations as Jonathan Ross responds
content.shortHeadline: Walliams allegations revisited in ITV documentary
content.standfirst: A Guardian and ITV News investigation is accompanied by a documentary featuring women’s accounts of alleged grooming and inappropriate behaviour. David Walliams denies wrongdoing; Jonathan Ross says he was unaware of the conduct alleged.

image.caption: David Walliams in 2024.

sources.originalTitle: David Walliams: Power and Silence review – some of this footage will make your head spin
Jonathan Ross ‘horrified’ by David Walliams and Russell Brand revelations

segments.body: The ITVX documentary Power and Silence accompanies a three-year investigation by the Guardian and ITV News into allegations by multiple women that David Walliams pursued them when they were teenagers or young adults and behaved inappropriately. Walliams denies the allegations, including sexual harassment and workplace misconduct.

segments.title: Responses and consequences
segments.body: Jonathan Ross has said he was “genuinely unaware” of Walliams’s conduct, despite making a 2004 joke about the comedian going home with a 15-year-old. Ross says he believed the line referred to Walliams’s publicly reported dating history and calls it tasteless. The reporting also records professional consequences, including the BBC reviewing its material featuring Walliams and Sky dropping the licence for a film he wrote and starred in.

content.headline: Rivals’ return brings grief and consequence beneath the lavish romp
content.shortHeadline: Rivals finds poignancy amid the sex and scandal
content.standfirst: The second half of the drama’s latest season keeps its outrageous romances and rivalries, but the review finds more lasting consequences and moments of grief than before.

image.caption: Aidan Turner, Catriona Chandler and Danny Dyer in Rivals.

sources.originalTitle: Rivals review – this TV joy is so much more than just a romp

segments.body: Rivals returns after Monica’s death, with the competition between Corinium and Venturer continuing alongside affairs, betrayals and family entanglements. The review says the familiar comic excess remains, but the new episodes give more weight to the consequences of characters’ choices.

segments.title: A darker turn
segments.body: David Tennant’s Tony becomes more volatile as he grieves, while the review singles out Monica’s death scene as a moment of genuine heartbreak. It argues that the series is more than a romp, though the accumulation of grief sometimes dims the fun that made it distinctive.

content.headline: The Rings of Power’s third season adds romance but still struggles to engage
content.shortHeadline: The Rings of Power adds spectacle but remains a slog
content.standfirst: A five-year time jump brings Gandalf, the forged rings and new characters further into the story. The review welcomes the added action and romance but questions whether the fantasy prequel can win back viewers.

image.caption: Jamie Campbell Bower as Celeborn and Morfydd Clark as Galadriel in The Rings of Power.

sources.originalTitle: The Lord of the Rings: The Rings of Power season three review – this dull show’s revamp is too little, too late

segments.body: The third season of The Lord of the Rings: The Rings of Power picks up after the fall of Eregion, with Sauron building his power and other peoples of Middle-earth scattered across different fronts. Gandalf is more prominent, the rings are in play and the Harfoots have been sidelined.

segments.title: A relaunch under pressure
segments.body: The review sees the season as a soft relaunch, adding action, new characters and a romance between Galadriel and Celeborn. It finds the world-building and production design impressive but says the many separated plotlines still make the show feel closed-off and dramatically dull to viewers who are not already invested in Tolkien’s world.

content.headline: Inside the TV writers’ room, where collaboration and conflict shape a series
content.shortHeadline: TV writers’ rooms turn collaboration into story
content.standfirst: The Guardian’s film critic reflects on co-writing a new thriller and asks established showrunners how a writers’ room works. They describe a process that can be energising, competitive and difficult to lead.

image.caption: A scene from Hunting Alice Bell.

sources.originalTitle: ‘Like leading brave soldiers to certain death’: Succession’s Jesse Armstrong and more on the rollercoaster of TV writers’ rooms

segments.body: Writing for television can begin in a room where a team maps out plot beats and character arcs before individual writers draft episodes. The Guardian critic describes joining the room for Hunting Alice Bell, a Channel 4 thriller about a sports-centre manager targeted by online accusations and digital mob rule.

segments.title: The showrunner’s call
segments.body: Jesse Armstrong, creator of Succession, says a room can feel full of promise but can become dispiriting when a story stalls. He describes the showrunner’s responsibility to decide which direction to pursue. Other writers in the piece say rooms can range from supportive collaboration to competitive environments where writers feel they must fight to contribute.

content.headline: Manhood asks what a penis-enlargement clinic can—and cannot—fix
content.shortHeadline: Manhood looks beyond penis enlargement to men’s insecurities
content.standfirst: Daniel Lombroso’s documentary follows patients at a Dallas clinic offering injections to increase penis girth. The review finds stories of trauma, shame and self-image beneath the procedure, without a simple answer.

image.caption: David Smith, one of the patients in Manhood.

sources.originalTitle: Manhood review – a mind-boggling visit to the penis enlargement doctor who promises ‘better sex than ever’

segments.body: Manhood follows men seeking PhalloFill injections at a Dallas clinic run by Bill Moore. The treatment uses hyaluronic acid to increase girth, but the review finds the film more interested in what patients hope it will change about their lives than in the procedure itself.

segments.title: More than a cosmetic fix
segments.body: The film’s patients speak about porn, body image, shame and sexuality. The review describes Ruben’s account of childhood sexual assault as a turning point in understanding his story, and notes that another patient came to Moore after a previous enlargement procedure left him with hard lumps. It concludes that the problems explored in the film are more complex than a cosmetic treatment can solve.

content.headline: Black Doves’ cast and creator discuss the spy drama’s violent moral grey areas
content.shortHeadline: Black Doves pairs spy-thriller violence with human drama
content.standfirst: Keira Knightley, Ambika Mod and creator Joe Barton discuss a new season that sends its agents into further danger. They explain how humour and intimate character moments complicate the show’s gleeful violence.

image.caption: Keira Knightley as Helen Webb in Black Doves.

sources.originalTitle: Keira Knightley on Black Doves: ‘The violence is like a video game’

segments.body: Black Doves returns with Helen Webb, played by Keira Knightley, facing more dangerous missions after her husband becomes prime minister. Her handler Elizabeth Reed is missing, while hitman Sam must work through a kill list. Ambika Mod joins as rogue agent Laila Joshi, a reluctant ally to Helen.

segments.title: Making violence matter
segments.body: Knightley describes the show’s action as almost video-game-like, but says Joe Barton’s writing can bring an individual death into focus and make it disturbing. Barton says audiences are accustomed to violence in spy stories; the series tries to acknowledge that moral grey area while keeping its compromised characters compelling.

content.headline: Maya Jama’s next move tests whether television can still make a presenter
content.shortHeadline: Maya Jama leaves Love Island for a new Netflix chapter
content.standfirst: After leaving Love Island and signing a Netflix deal, Jama has a larger audience and a less certain path. The i Paper’s analysis argues that the presenter’s next challenge is finding a new format to make her own.

image.caption: Maya Jama, who has announced she is leaving Love Island.

sources.originalTitle: Maya Jama belongs to a dying breed of presenters

segments.body: Maya Jama is leaving Love Island after nine series across four years and has signed a deal with Netflix, which says projects are in development. Her recent appearance on Celebrity Traitors reached a wider audience than the start of this year’s Love Island, according to the commentary.

segments.title: Finding a format
segments.body: The piece argues that traditional television offers fewer established programmes for a new presenter to inherit, while launching an original format has become difficult. It suggests Netflix may give Jama room to build a programme around her own style, but notes that details of the deal have not yet been announced.

content.headline: Doctor Who’s future is uncertain after the Disney+ partnership ends
content.shortHeadline: Doctor Who faces an uncertain future off screen
content.standfirst: The BBC has ended its Disney+ collaboration, cancelled a planned Christmas special and is seeking a new production partner. Fans and writers debate what went wrong—and what the long-running series needs next.

image.caption: Several actors who have played the Doctor, including Peter Capaldi, David Tennant, Ncuti Gatwa and Jodie Whittaker.

sources.originalTitle: The sad, slow death of Doctor Who

segments.body: After Ncuti Gatwa’s run as the Fifteenth Doctor ended in 2025, the BBC and Disney+ partnership has been discontinued. The BBC cancelled a planned Christmas special and is seeking another company to help fund future production, but no new partner or Doctor has been announced.

segments.title: A changing institution
segments.body: The article traces the programme’s earlier cancellation in 1989 and revival in 2005, then considers recent criticism of its scripts, casting and direction. Lifelong fan Frank Skinner says he worries the show has been kept off air for too long; former writer Nina Metivier points to kindness and curiosity as core values worth preserving. The future remains unresolved.

content.headline: Grand Theft Auto’s cultural reach goes far beyond crime and car chases
content.shortHeadline: How Grand Theft Auto became a cultural colossus
content.standfirst: As GTA VI approaches, a feature traces how Rockstar built detailed, satirical worlds from film, music and city life. A companion look at the series’ movie influences shows how it has borrowed from—and fed back into—popular culture.

image.caption: Lucia and Jason, the protagonists of Grand Theft Auto VI.

sources.originalTitle: Crime pays: how Grand Theft Auto became a cultural colossus
‘It’s so glossy and sexy!’: 10 movies (and one TV show) that inspired Grand Theft Auto

segments.body: Grand Theft Auto grew from a 1997 game about stealing cars in imagined US cities into a vast open-world series. The feature argues that its cultural reach comes not only from crime and cinematic references, but from the freedom to inhabit densely observed cities and discover incidental details between missions.

segments.title: A dialogue with film
segments.body: A related feature traces influences including Scarface, Miami Vice, Goodfellas, Boyz n the Hood and Bonnie and Clyde. It also describes the traffic in influence running both ways: Rockstar has drawn on film and television, while later filmmakers have reflected the series’ own style and imagery.

content.headline: Ocarina of Time’s remake delights, and its midnight launch brings fans together
content.shortHeadline: Ocarina of Time remake revives a shared gaming ritual
content.standfirst: The Switch 2 remake updates a landmark Zelda game while preserving its melancholy, according to the review. A separate report from London’s midnight launch finds the appeal of meeting fellow fans—and the frustration of a long queue.

image.caption: The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time on Switch 2.

sources.originalTitle: The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time review – a dream come true
The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time has revived the midnight game launch – but was it worth the wait?
