segments.body: The Switch 2 remake of The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time keeps the original game’s world, puzzles and story structure while adding voiced scenes, expanded dialogue, updated controls and an orchestral score. The review praises the result as a reinvention that makes the 1998 game feel vivid without losing its melancholy.

segments.title: A night in the queue
segments.body: At a London midnight launch, hundreds of fans waited for early copies and exclusive collectibles. The Guardian’s reporter describes the shared excitement of the gathering, but also the disappointment of a queue that moved so slowly that some customers left their details to receive the promised box by post.

content.headline: Can Alex Garland make Elden Ring work as a Hollywood fantasy film?
content.shortHeadline: Elden Ring adaptation faces a formidable challenge
content.standfirst: The game’s scale, horror and sparse storytelling make it a difficult world to translate for film. The project is reportedly shot and in post-production, but its budget and distribution plans remain uncertain.

image.caption: Elden Ring.

sources.originalTitle: Alex Garland’s Elden Ring adaptation is on course to be Hollywood’s goriest ever fantasy movie

segments.body: Alex Garland’s adaptation of Elden Ring is in post-production, according to the article, with a cast including Cailee Spaeny, Ben Whishaw and Nick Offerman. The game has sold more than 30 million copies and is widely regarded as a major work of fantasy, raising expectations for a film that must make its world matter to viewers unfamiliar with the game.

segments.title: A world without easy answers
segments.body: The feature argues that Elden Ring’s grotesque creatures, sprawling mythology and bleak tone pose a different challenge from more conventional fantasy adaptations. It says a reported budget near $200m could leave Garland less room for the ambiguity found in earlier films, while the movie’s plot and final form remain unknown.

content.headline: Blood test signal may reveal ovarian precancer before tumours form
content.shortHeadline: Blood signal may detect ovarian precancer before tumours form
content.standfirst: A study found that levels of an RNA molecule in blood could help identify a precursor to ovarian cancer. The result is promising, but the research does not establish a screening test for general use.

sources.originalTitle: Molecular signal in blood helps detect early risk for ovarian cancer, study finds

segments.body: The study examined Tu-Stroma, an RNA molecule found at higher levels in the blood of women with serous tubal intraepithelial carcinoma (STIC), a precancerous condition that can precede ovarian cancer. Researchers detected STIC in 92.3% of affected women and correctly identified 98.2% of healthy women in their study.

segments.title: What the results could mean
segments.body: For women with inherited risk factors, the researchers reported that about 72% of positive results would be accurate, while nearly 100% of negative results would be correct. A blood test that could indicate whether precancerous lesions are present might eventually inform difficult decisions about preventive surgery. Its performance and usefulness in wider clinical practice remain to be established.

content.headline: New obesity criteria could correct millions of BMI diagnoses
content.shortHeadline: A broader obesity test could correct millions of BMI diagnoses
content.standfirst: An analysis of health records suggests BMI alone can miss excess body fat or label some people incorrectly. The proposed approach adds body measurements and checks whether fat is affecting organ function.

sources.originalTitle: BMI alternative for identifying obesity ‘could prevent misdiagnosis in millions’

segments.body: An analysis of records from more than 800,000 people in the UK, US, China and Spain suggests that BMI alone misses obesity in 5–9% of adults and wrongly diagnoses it in as many as 3%. The proposed approach combines BMI with waist measurements or waist-to-height ratio to assess excess body fat.

segments.title: Risk is not the same as disease
segments.body: The approach also distinguishes clinical obesity, where excess body fat is already impairing organ function, from pre-clinical obesity, where it presents a risk but has not yet caused those problems. The researchers report that 80–90% of people with pre-clinical obesity did not progress to clinical obesity over the following 10 years. The method is more involved for clinicians, and the article does not establish how widely it will be adopted.

content.headline: Small baxdrostat follow-up hints at lasting effect on some hypertension
content.shortHeadline: Small study hints baxdrostat’s blood-pressure effect may last
content.standfirst: In a follow-up involving 14 patients, blood pressure stayed lower for up to two years after they stopped the drug. Researchers say a larger study is needed before claiming a limited course can provide a lasting cure.

sources.originalTitle: New drug that could permanently cure high blood pressure coming to UK by 2027

segments.body: Baxdrostat is designed to block production of aldosterone, a hormone that can raise blood pressure. An analysis following 14 patients from a larger trial found that their blood pressure remained lower for up to two years after they stopped taking the drug, following six to 12 months of treatment.

segments.title: A finding still to prove
segments.body: The researchers suggest the drug may affect cells that overproduce aldosterone in some people with benign adrenal tumours. The small follow-up does not prove a permanent cure: one researcher said a larger study now under way is needed to establish whether the effect lasts. The drug’s UK availability and NHS use are also not settled in the report.

content.headline: US tests autonomous mine-hunting systems as Gulf shipping faces risk
content.shortHeadline: Autonomous systems take on mine-hunting as Gulf shipping faces risk
content.standfirst: Robotic boats and underwater vehicles can search for mines while keeping sailors farther from danger. They can reduce risk, experts say, but cannot prove that a route is clear.

sources.originalTitle: Robot vessels take on the dangerous work of mine hunting

segments.body: Mine-hunting has traditionally relied on specialist ships and crews. Newer systems, monitored by people on shore, use sonar and sensors to search the seabed; some build three-dimensional images that software can analyse for objects resembling mines. The latest Gulf conflict is providing a test for more capable US systems, though the military has disclosed limited details.

segments.title: Reducing, not removing, risk
segments.body: Uncrewed systems can keep sailors out of immediate danger and may be deployed with smaller teams. But, as a former Royal Navy robotics officer put it, operators “can't prove the negative” that no mines are present; they can only reduce the risk. The report says the US considers the Omani route cleared and that shipments are running at about 75% of pre-conflict levels, while uncertainty about the threat remains.

content.headline: Germany reportedly bars Chinese drones from military sites over security fears
content.shortHeadline: Germany reportedly bans Chinese drones at military sites
content.standfirst: Reports say Germany is withdrawing commercially available Chinese-made drones from military bases and training grounds. The move reflects wider security concerns, but the reporting identifies no specific threat from the drones.

sources.originalTitle: Germany reportedly bans Chinese drones at military bases over security concerns

segments.body: Germany has reportedly banned Chinese-made commercial drones from military bases and training grounds, with units told to withdraw them as quickly as possible. Der Spiegel reported that individual military units had bought drones, including models from DJI, with limited oversight and no central record of purchases.

segments.title: Concern without a named threat
segments.body: The report places the move alongside other restrictions and warnings about connected vehicles and devices, based on fears that sensors could expose sensitive information. US military officials have not identified a specific threat in the cited vehicle case. BYD, responding to concerns about its cars, says data processed or stored by its vehicles cannot be remotely accessed from China.

content.headline: UK under-16 social media rules could reach YouTube Kids and Spotify
content.shortHeadline: Proposed UK rules could put YouTube Kids and Spotify in scope
content.standfirst: The UK government is considering a broad definition of platforms that could bring services not usually thought of as social media within an under-16 ban. The final scope and exemptions are not yet settled.

sources.originalTitle: UK social media ban expansion for under-16s could cover YouTube Kids

segments.body: Draft rules could bring as many as 150 platforms into the UK’s under-16 social media ban, according to sources briefed on the proposals. Services potentially affected include YouTube Kids, Spotify and Lego Play, because the government is considering recommender systems and user-generated content as part of its approach.

segments.title: Scope and an possible exit
segments.body: The government had said educational, shopping and music-streaming services would be exempt, but industry representatives say a broad test leaves platforms unsure whether they would be covered. Ministers say services could fall outside the rules if they remove harmful features, although companies argue that removing recommendation systems could undermine how their services work. The regulations are still under consideration.

content.headline: AI data-centre plans could add vast gas capacity as UK sites face local disputes
content.shortHeadline: AI data centres could drive major gas buildout and local opposition
content.standfirst: A BloombergNEF analysis says planned on-site gas plants could add 181GW of capacity across the US and Europe as data centres wait for grid connections. A proposed east London campus shows how the expansion is also colliding with local concerns.

image.caption: Fields proposed for a data-centre campus in North Ockendon, east London.

sources.originalTitle: AI datacentres plan on-site power stations on huge scale despite climate risks, research reveals
'We all need data, but do we need the largest data centre in Europe here?'

segments.body: Data-centre projects in the US, UK and mainland Europe have proposed 181GW of on-site gas-fired capacity, according to BloombergNEF, citing delays to grid connections. If built, the planned capacity would emit an estimated 345 million tonnes of carbon-dioxide equivalent annually in the US, where 90% of the on-site gas plants are proposed. The report warns that facilities described as temporary could keep generating power after grid connections arrive.

segments.title: A local test of the expansion
segments.body: In North Ockendon, east London, developers Digital Reef have proposed a large data-centre campus on green-belt land. Local residents raise concerns about construction, noise and pressure on electricity and water supplies. The developer says the project would bring jobs and public green space; a London planning report identifies grid capacity and water use as constraints on growth. The proposal has not yet been approved.

content.headline: AI use puts university coursework under pressure as regulator urges exams
content.shortHeadline: Regulator urges more exams as AI challenges university assessment
content.standfirst: England’s higher education regulator says some students can complete assessments with AI in minutes and evade detection. Universities are changing how they grade work, while student representatives argue that traditional methods also need reform.

sources.originalTitle: AI has made it ‘close to impossible’ to assess university coursework, regulator says
Students passing university assessments in minutes using AI, regulator warns

segments.body: Research by England’s Office for Students and Advance HE, based on interviews and surveys involving staff and students at at least 127 institutions, found that some assessments can be completed to a high standard with AI in minutes. The regulator says AI use can be difficult to detect and warns that assessments may fail to measure students’ own knowledge and skills.

segments.title: Changing how students are assessed
segments.body: The regulator points to closed-book and practical exams, in-person presentations and oral exams as ways to assess learning without relying on unsupervised written work. Universities UK says institutions are already adapting with a mix of exams, process-based work and controlled AI use. The National Union of Students argues that some traditional assessment methods are themselves outdated and should be redesigned with students.

perspectives.body: The National Union of Students says AI is exposing weaknesses in traditional learning methods, including essay questions, handouts and slideshows, and calls for innovative approaches developed with students.

content.headline: New York starts registering major AI developers under safety law
content.shortHeadline: New York opens registration for major AI developers
content.standfirst: A state safety law will require large frontier AI companies to publish safety frameworks and report critical incidents. New York has opened registration ahead of the rules taking effect at the start of 2027.

sources.originalTitle: OpenAI, Anthropic face new oversight as New York’s AI safety law takes effect

segments.body: New York has opened a registration portal for major frontier AI developers, which must register by 1 January 2027 under the RAISE Act. The law applies to companies with more than $500m in annual revenue and requires published safety frameworks, public model transparency reports and reports of critical safety incidents within 72 hours.

segments.title: Enforcement and oversight
segments.body: The state’s new Office of Digital Innovation, Governance, Integrity, and Trust will oversee the law. Penalties can reach $1m for a first violation and $3m for later violations. New York has also launched a research centre to evaluate advanced AI systems and review companies’ safety frameworks; other states have adopted or are developing similar measures.

content.headline: Tamil Nadu library investigation raises questions over alleged AI-generated book
content.shortHeadline: Tamil Nadu probes library book purchases amid AI allegations
content.standfirst: A court has ordered an investigation into disputed public-library purchases in Tamil Nadu. Writers have raised concerns about questionable authorship and errors, but it remains unclear whether AI was used to produce any of the books.

image.caption: The newly opened Periyar Arivulagam library is at the centre of the allegations.

sources.originalTitle: New Indian mega library rocked by scandal over 'AI-generated books'

segments.body: The Madras High Court has ordered an anti-corruption investigation into books bought for a new public library in Coimbatore, after novelist Perumal Murugan questioned their authorship and accuracy. The state government has ordered an audit of library collections, and officials say 523 books have been removed from Chennai’s Connemara Public Library following preliminary checks.

segments.title: What remains unproven
segments.body: The allegations have prompted scrutiny of the procurement process and concern about how libraries can verify books as AI-generated material spreads. The BBC report says it is not clear whether AI was used to create any of the disputed titles. Tamil Nadu’s government blames the previous administration for the purchases; the DMK denies wrongdoing and says the allegations are politically motivated.

content.headline: Startup bets on simulations to make AI agents more reliable
content.shortHeadline: Startup uses simulations to tackle AI-agent failures
content.standfirst: Plurai says it can test AI agents against simulated versions of a company’s systems and use the results to improve performance. The approach addresses a known reliability challenge, but the claimed gains and cost savings remain company claims.

sources.originalTitle: Plurai wants to help AI agents work better using the same approach that helped get self-driving cars to roads

segments.body: AI agents can fail on complex tasks, according to benchmarks cited in the report: one evaluation found leading systems succeeding on fewer than 83 of 100 tasks, while a simulated corporate test recorded 76.8% accuracy for its best-performing model. Startup Plurai says it is adapting techniques used to test self-driving systems to help agents handle unusual situations before they encounter them in business.

segments.title: Testing against a company’s systems
segments.body: Plurai builds a digital twin of the software, information and tools an agent would use, then maps possible task flows to identify edge cases. The startup says it can use those results to train smaller open-weight models and, in tests with Nvidia and Nebius, outperform some mid-tier frontier models at lower cost. Those results are not independent evidence of performance in wider deployment.
